chapter_text:
CHAPTER 12 - SOURCES OF ENERGY

Introduction

Energy is the capacity to do work. Every activity of daily life - cooking food, lighting homes, running machines, driving vehicles, generating electricity - requires energy. As populations grow and industries expand, the demand for energy rises sharply. The original source of almost all the energy we use is the Sun, either directly (as sunlight) or indirectly (stored in fossil fuels, wind, flowing water and biomass). This chapter examines what makes a source of energy useful, surveys the conventional (non-renewable) and non-conventional (renewable) sources available to us, and discusses the environmental consequences of energy use and the need for energy conservation.

12.1 CHARACTERISTICS OF A GOOD SOURCE OF ENERGY

A good source of energy should:
 - Release a LARGE amount of energy per unit mass or volume (high energy density).
 - Be EASILY available and present in plenty.
 - Be EASY and SAFE to store and to transport.
 - Be ECONOMICAL (cheap to obtain and use).
 - Cause LITTLE OR NO POLLUTION when used.
No single real source meets all these conditions perfectly, so we use a combination of sources.

Sources of energy are broadly classified as:
 - CONVENTIONAL (non-renewable) sources: fossil fuels (coal, petroleum, natural gas) and nuclear fuels. They have been in use for a long time and exist in limited stock - once used up they cannot be replaced within a human timescale.
 - NON-CONVENTIONAL (renewable) sources: solar, wind, hydro, tidal, wave, ocean thermal, geothermal and biomass energy. They are continuously replenished by nature and will not run out.

12.2 FOSSIL FUELS

Fossil fuels - COAL, PETROLEUM and NATURAL GAS - were formed over millions of years from the remains of dead plants and animals buried under sediment and subjected to high pressure and temperature in the absence of air. Because they take so long to form, they are NON-RENEWABLE.

(a) Coal was formed from the remains of large land plants that grew in swamps millions of years ago. It is mainly carbon. Coal is burnt in homes and industries and is used in thermal power plants to generate electricity.

(b) Petroleum (crude oil) was formed from the remains of tiny marine plants and animals. It is found trapped between rock layers. By fractional distillation in a refinery, crude oil is separated into useful fractions: petrol, diesel, kerosene, LPG, lubricating oil, paraffin wax and bitumen. Petroleum products fuel almost all transport.

(c) Natural gas is found above petroleum deposits. It is mainly methane (CH4). Compressed Natural Gas (CNG) is used as a cleaner fuel for vehicles, and natural gas is also piped to homes as a domestic fuel.

Limitations and pollution from fossil fuels:
 - They are LIMITED in quantity and will be exhausted.
 - Burning them releases CARBON DIOXIDE (CO2), a greenhouse gas that causes GLOBAL WARMING.
 - They release oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (SO2, NO2) which cause ACID RAIN.
 - Incomplete combustion produces carbon monoxide (CO) and soot, which harm health.

12.3 THERMAL POWER PLANTS

In a THERMAL POWER PLANT, fossil fuel (usually coal) is burnt to heat water and produce high-pressure steam. The steam turns a TURBINE, which is connected to a GENERATOR that produces electricity. The chain of energy conversions is:
   chemical energy (fuel) -> heat energy (steam) -> mechanical energy (turbine) -> electrical energy (generator).
Thermal plants are usually set up near coalfields or oil fields to reduce the cost of transporting fuel. Their drawback is the pollution from burning large amounts of fuel.

12.4 SOLAR ENERGY

The Sun radiates enormous energy; a tiny fraction reaches the Earth and is the ultimate source of most of our energy. Solar energy is free, inexhaustible and pollution-free, but it is dilute (spread over a large area), available only during the day and affected by clouds.

Devices that use solar energy:
 - SOLAR COOKER: a box-type cooker has an insulated box painted black inside, a glass sheet cover and a plane mirror reflector. Sunlight enters through the glass; the black surface absorbs it and gets hot; the glass traps the heat (greenhouse effect). Temperatures of about 100-140 degrees C are reached - enough to cook food, but slowly and only in sunshine.
 - SOLAR CELL (photovoltaic cell): made of semiconductors such as silicon. It converts sunlight DIRECTLY into electricity. A single cell gives a small voltage; many cells joined together form a SOLAR PANEL. Solar cells power calculators, satellites, street lights and remote homes. They have no moving parts and need little maintenance, but are costly to make.
 - SOLAR WATER HEATER: uses an insulated tank and blackened pipes/collector to absorb sunlight and heat water for domestic use.

12.5 WIND ENERGY

Moving air (wind) possesses kinetic energy. A WINDMILL has large blades mounted on a tall tower; the wind rotates the blades, and this rotary motion can pump water or, in a WIND GENERATOR, turn a turbine to produce electricity. A large number of windmills set up together form a WIND ENERGY FARM. For useful generation the wind speed should be above about 15 km/h. Wind energy is clean and renewable, but it needs windy locations, large open areas and a high initial cost; output also varies with the wind.

12.6 HYDRO ENERGY (HYDROELECTRIC POWER)

The kinetic energy of flowing or falling water can be used to generate electricity. A DAM is built across a river to store water at a height, giving it potential energy. When the water is allowed to fall, its potential energy becomes kinetic energy; the fast-moving water turns a turbine connected to a generator. This is HYDROELECTRIC POWER. It is renewable and pollution-free, but building dams submerges large areas of land and forests, displaces people and affects aquatic life.

12.7 ENERGY FROM THE SEA

(a) TIDAL ENERGY: the rise and fall of sea water due to tides can be harnessed. A dam is built across a narrow opening to the sea; water flows in and out through turbines as tides rise and fall, generating electricity. Suitable sites are limited.

(b) WAVE ENERGY: the kinetic energy of sea waves (produced by winds over the ocean) can drive turbines. It is useful only where strong waves occur.

(c) OCEAN THERMAL ENERGY (OTEC): the surface water of the ocean is warmer than the deep water. An Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion plant uses this TEMPERATURE DIFFERENCE (about 20 degrees C between the warm surface and the cold depths) to boil a volatile liquid (such as ammonia); the vapour runs a turbine, and the cold deep water condenses it again.

12.8 GEOTHERMAL ENERGY

The heat inside the Earth (in regions of HOT SPOTS) can heat underground water into steam. Where this steam reaches near the surface, it can be tapped through pipes and used to run turbines and generate electricity. Geothermal energy is renewable and clean, but only a few locations have usable hot spots.

12.9 BIOMASS AND BIOGAS

BIOMASS is organic matter from plants and animals - wood, crop residues, cow dung and other wastes. When burnt directly, wood and dung release heat but cause smoke and pollution and give little usable energy.

BIOGAS (also called GOBAR GAS) is a much cleaner fuel produced from biomass by the action of microorganisms in the ABSENCE of air (anaerobic decomposition). Biogas is a mixture of gases of which about 65-75% is METHANE (CH4), which burns without smoke.

A BIOGAS (GOBAR GAS) PLANT consists of:
 - A MIXING TANK where cow dung is mixed with water to form a slurry.
 - A DIGESTER (a sealed, dome-shaped underground tank) where the slurry is fermented by anaerobic bacteria over a few weeks, producing biogas.
 - A GAS OUTLET at the top through which the gas is drawn off by pipes.
 - An OUTLET TANK and OVERFLOW for the spent slurry, which is removed and used as excellent manure (rich in nitrogen and phosphorus).

Advantages of biogas:
 - It is a clean, smokeless fuel with a high heat output.
 - It is made from waste (dung, agricultural waste) - a renewable resource.
 - The leftover slurry is a good fertiliser.
 - It provides a safe way of disposing of animal and human waste, improving sanitation.

12.10 NUCLEAR ENERGY

Nuclear energy is the energy released from the nucleus of an atom. There are two processes:
 - NUCLEAR FISSION: the nucleus of a heavy atom such as uranium-235 SPLITS into smaller nuclei when struck by a neutron, releasing a very large amount of energy and more neutrons. These neutrons split further nuclei - a CHAIN REACTION. Fission is the process used in nuclear power plants.
 - NUCLEAR FUSION: two light nuclei (such as hydrogen) JOIN to form a heavier nucleus, releasing even more energy. Fusion powers the Sun and stars, but is very hard to control on Earth.

A NUCLEAR POWER PLANT uses a controlled fission chain reaction in a REACTOR. The heat produced converts water into steam, which drives a turbine and a generator to produce electricity - the same final stage as a thermal plant, but the heat comes from fission, not from burning fuel.

Advantages of nuclear energy:
 - A very small amount of nuclear fuel releases an enormous amount of energy.
 - It does not release carbon dioxide or smoke during operation.

Hazards of nuclear energy:
 - It produces RADIOACTIVE WASTE that remains dangerous for a very long time and must be stored safely.
 - Accidents (leaks) can release harmful radiation.
 - The radiation can cause serious damage to living tissue and the environment.

12.11 ENVIRONMENTAL CONSEQUENCES AND ENERGY CONSERVATION

All forms of energy use affect the environment. Burning fossil fuels causes air pollution, acid rain and global warming; dams alter ecosystems and displace people; nuclear plants produce radioactive waste. Therefore we must use energy WISELY.

ENERGY CONSERVATION means using energy efficiently and avoiding waste. Simple measures include: switching off lights, fans and appliances when not in use; using energy-efficient devices (CFL/LED lamps, star-rated appliances); using public transport, cycling or walking; insulating buildings; and shifting wherever possible to renewable sources. Conserving energy saves money, reduces pollution and makes our limited fossil-fuel reserves last longer.

SUMMARY

- A good source of energy gives much energy per unit mass, is easily and cheaply available, safe to store and transport, and causes little pollution.
- Conventional (non-renewable) sources - coal, petroleum, natural gas and nuclear fuel - are limited and (the fossil fuels) polluting. Fossil fuels formed over millions of years from buried plant and animal remains.
- A thermal power plant burns fuel to make steam that drives a turbine and generator: chemical -> heat -> mechanical -> electrical energy.
- Non-conventional (renewable) sources include solar (solar cooker, solar cell/panel, solar water heater), wind (windmills, wind farms), hydro (dams), tidal/wave/ocean thermal (OTEC), and geothermal energy.
- Biomass gives biogas (gobar gas), about 65-75% methane, made by anaerobic decomposition in a digester; it is a clean fuel and the leftover slurry is good manure.
- Nuclear energy comes from fission (splitting of heavy nuclei, used in reactors) or fusion (joining of light nuclei, powering the Sun). It gives huge energy from little fuel but produces dangerous radioactive waste.
- All energy use has environmental costs, so we must conserve energy by using it efficiently and shifting to renewable sources.

chapter_summary.title: Sources of Energy - Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This is the NIOS Class 10 Science & Technology (212) Learner's Guide summary for Lesson 12. It explains what makes a good source of energy, surveys the conventional (non-renewable) fossil and nuclear fuels and the non-conventional (renewable) sources - solar, wind, hydro, tidal, wave, ocean thermal, geothermal and biomass - describes the thermal, nuclear and biogas systems, and stresses the environmental consequences of energy use and the need for energy conservation.

sections.heading: Characteristics and classification of energy sources
bullets: A good source of energy releases a large amount of energy per unit mass or volume, is easily and cheaply available, and is safe to store and transport.
It should also cause little or no pollution. No real source satisfies every condition, so a combination of sources is used.

Conventional (non-renewable) sources - coal, petroleum, natural gas and nuclear fuels - are limited in stock; non-conventional (renewable) sources - solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal and biomass - are continuously replenished by nature.

sections.heading: Fossil fuels and the thermal power plant
bullets: Coal, petroleum and natural gas formed over millions of years from the remains of dead plants and animals buried under high pressure and temperature, so they are non-renewable.
Burning fossil fuels releases carbon dioxide (global warming), oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (acid rain) and carbon monoxide/soot (health hazards).
In a thermal power plant, fuel is burnt to make steam that turns a turbine and a generator: chemical energy -> heat energy -> mechanical energy -> electrical energy.

sections.heading: Solar energy and its devices
bullets: A box-type solar cooker has a blackened insulated box, a glass cover and a plane mirror reflector; sunlight is absorbed and trapped by the greenhouse effect to cook food slowly.
A solar cell (photovoltaic cell) made of silicon converts sunlight directly into electricity; many cells joined form a solar panel that has no moving parts.
Solar energy is free, clean and inexhaustible, but it is dilute, available only in daytime and affected by clouds; solar devices have a high initial cost.

sections.heading: Wind, hydro, sea and geothermal energy
bullets: A windmill uses the kinetic energy of moving air to turn blades; many windmills together form a wind energy farm that can generate electricity where winds are strong.
Hydroelectric power uses water stored at a height behind a dam; falling water turns a turbine and generator, but dams submerge land and displace people.

Tidal energy uses the rise and fall of tides, wave energy uses sea waves, OTEC uses the temperature difference between warm surface and cold deep ocean water, and geothermal energy taps steam from hot spots inside the Earth.

sections.heading: Biomass, biogas and nuclear energy
bullets: Biogas (gobar gas) is produced from cow dung and waste by anaerobic decomposition in a sealed digester; it is about 65-75% methane and burns without smoke, and the leftover slurry is good manure.
Nuclear fission splits a heavy nucleus (uranium-235) releasing huge energy in a chain reaction; this is used in nuclear reactors. Nuclear fusion joins light nuclei and powers the Sun.
Nuclear energy gives enormous energy from little fuel and emits no CO2, but produces dangerous radioactive waste; all energy use has environmental costs, so energy must be conserved.

key_takeaways: A good energy source gives much energy per unit mass, is cheap and easily available, safe to store and transport, and causes little pollution.
Coal, petroleum and natural gas are fossil fuels formed over millions of years from buried remains; they are non-renewable and polluting.
A thermal power plant converts chemical energy of fuel into heat, then mechanical (turbine) and finally electrical energy (generator).
Solar devices include the solar cooker (greenhouse effect), the solar cell/panel (sunlight to electricity) and the solar water heater.
Renewable sources also include wind, hydro (dams), tidal, wave, ocean thermal (OTEC) and geothermal energy.
Biogas (gobar gas) is a clean fuel (about 65-75% methane) made by anaerobic decomposition; the leftover slurry is good manure.
Nuclear energy from fission or fusion gives huge energy from little fuel but creates radioactive waste, so energy must be used wisely and conserved.

glossary.definition: A material or natural process from which energy can be obtained in a usable form, such as fuels, sunlight, wind or flowing water.
A source of energy that exists in a limited amount and cannot be replaced within a human timescale once used up, e.g. coal, petroleum, natural gas, nuclear fuel.
A source of energy that is continuously replenished by nature and will not run out, e.g. solar, wind, hydro, tidal, geothermal and biomass energy.
A fuel (coal, petroleum or natural gas) formed over millions of years from the buried remains of dead plants and animals under high pressure and temperature.
A plant that burns fuel to heat water into steam, which turns a turbine and generator to produce electricity (chemical -> heat -> mechanical -> electrical).
A box-type device with a blackened insulated box, glass cover and mirror reflector that absorbs and traps sunlight by the greenhouse effect to cook food.
A photovoltaic device, usually of silicon, that converts sunlight directly into electricity; many cells joined together form a solar panel.
A device whose blades are rotated by moving air; the rotation can pump water or drive a generator. Many windmills together form a wind energy farm.
Electricity generated when water stored at a height behind a dam falls and turns a turbine connected to a generator.
Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion - a system that uses the temperature difference between warm surface water and cold deep ocean water to run a turbine.
Energy obtained from the heat inside the Earth, where underground water is heated into steam at hot spots and used to drive turbines.
A clean fuel (about 65-75% methane) produced from cow dung and waste by anaerobic decomposition in a sealed digester.
The splitting of a heavy nucleus such as uranium-235 into smaller nuclei when struck by a neutron, releasing large energy and more neutrons (a chain reaction).
The joining of two light nuclei (such as hydrogen) to form a heavier nucleus, releasing very large energy; it is the process that powers the Sun.
Using energy efficiently and avoiding waste, e.g. switching off appliances, using efficient devices and shifting to renewable sources.

worksheet.title: Worksheet - Sources of Energy (NIOS Official)
worksheet.instructions: This is the NIOS Secondary Science & Technology (212) official Worksheet-12 for Lesson 12. Attempt all questions. Support your answers with reasons and diagrams where asked.

questions.question: List four characteristics of a good source of energy.
questions.answer: A good source of energy should: (1) release a LARGE amount of energy per unit mass or volume (high energy density); (2) be EASILY AVAILABLE in plenty; (3) be EASY and SAFE to STORE and TRANSPORT; and (4) be ECONOMICAL and cause LITTLE OR NO POLLUTION when used. No single real source satisfies all these conditions perfectly, so a combination of sources is used in practice.
questions.explanation: Recall the standard list of properties of an ideal energy source.

questions.question: How are fossil fuels formed, and why are they called non-renewable?
questions.answer:
Fossil fuels (coal, petroleum and natural gas) were formed over MILLIONS OF YEARS from the remains of dead plants and animals that were buried under layers of sediment and subjected to high pressure and high temperature in the absence of air. Coal came mainly from buried land plants; petroleum and natural gas came from tiny marine organisms.
They are called NON-RENEWABLE because they take millions of years to form, so once the existing reserves are used up they cannot be replaced within a human timescale. Their stock is limited and is being depleted faster than it can ever re-form.
questions.explanation: Formation from buried remains over millions of years; limited, slow-forming stock.

questions.question: Explain the working of a thermal power plant and state the energy conversions that take place in it.
questions.answer:
A THERMAL POWER PLANT generates electricity by burning a fossil fuel, usually coal.
Working: (1) Coal is burnt in a furnace/boiler. (2) The heat produced boils water and converts it into HIGH-PRESSURE STEAM. (3) The steam is directed onto the blades of a TURBINE, making it rotate. (4) The rotating turbine is connected to a GENERATOR, which produces electricity. (5) The used steam is cooled and condensed back to water to be reused.
Energy conversions: chemical energy (stored in the fuel) -> heat energy (in the steam) -> mechanical energy (rotation of the turbine) -> electrical energy (output of the generator).
Thermal plants are usually built near coalfields to reduce the cost of transporting fuel. Their main drawback is the large amount of pollution (CO2, SO2, NO2, soot) produced by burning fuel.
questions.explanation: Burn fuel -> steam -> turbine -> generator; chemical to heat to mechanical to electrical energy.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a box-type solar cooker.
questions.answer:
Construction: A box-type solar cooker is an insulated box that is painted BLACK on the inside, fitted with a GLASS SHEET cover on top and a PLANE MIRROR reflector hinged to the lid.
Working: The plane mirror reflects extra sunlight into the box. Sunlight enters through the glass and is absorbed by the black inner surface, which gets hot. The glass cover allows sunlight in but does not let the heat (infrared) escape easily - this is the GREENHOUSE EFFECT - so heat builds up inside. Temperatures of about 100-140 degrees C are reached, enough to cook food.
Limitations: it works only in bright sunshine, cooks slowly, cannot be used at night or on cloudy days, and cannot be used for frying or baking that need higher temperatures.
questions.explanation: Black box + glass cover + mirror; greenhouse effect traps heat to cook food.

questions.question: What is a solar cell? State two of its uses.
questions.answer:
A SOLAR CELL (photovoltaic cell) is a device made of a semiconductor such as SILICON that converts sunlight DIRECTLY into electricity. A single cell produces only a small voltage, so many cells are joined together to form a SOLAR PANEL that gives a usable amount of power.
Two uses: (1) providing electricity in artificial satellites and space probes; (2) powering calculators, street lights, traffic signals and remote homes that are far from the electricity grid. Solar cells have no moving parts and need little maintenance, but they are costly to manufacture.
questions.explanation: Semiconductor device, sunlight to electricity; satellites, calculators, remote homes.

questions.question: How is hydroelectric power generated? Mention one disadvantage of building large dams.
questions.answer:
Hydroelectric power uses the energy of falling water. A DAM is built across a river to store a large quantity of water at a HEIGHT, giving the water POTENTIAL ENERGY. When the water is allowed to fall through pipes, its potential energy changes into KINETIC ENERGY; the fast-moving water turns a TURBINE connected to a GENERATOR, which produces electricity.
It is renewable and pollution-free. One disadvantage: building a large dam submerges vast areas of land and forests, displaces people from their homes, and disturbs aquatic and other ecosystems.
questions.explanation: Water stored at height -> falls -> turbine -> generator; dams submerge land and displace people.

questions.question: Describe the construction and working of a biogas (gobar gas) plant. State two advantages of biogas.
questions.answer:
A BIOGAS (GOBAR GAS) PLANT produces clean fuel from cow dung and other biomass by ANAEROBIC decomposition (in the absence of air).
Construction and working: (1) Cow dung is mixed with water in a MIXING TANK to form a slurry. (2) The slurry flows into a sealed, dome-shaped underground DIGESTER. (3) Inside the digester, anaerobic bacteria ferment the slurry over a few weeks, producing BIOGAS - a mixture that is about 65-75% METHANE (CH4). (4) The gas collects at the top and is drawn off through a GAS OUTLET pipe for cooking or lighting. (5) The spent slurry leaves through an OUTLET/OVERFLOW tank and is used as manure.
Two advantages: (1) Biogas is a clean, smokeless fuel with a high heat output, produced from waste (a renewable resource); (2) the leftover slurry is an excellent fertiliser, rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, and the process gives a safe way to dispose of waste, improving sanitation.
questions.explanation: Mixing tank -> digester (anaerobic, ~65-75% methane) -> gas outlet -> slurry as manure.

questions.question: Distinguish between nuclear fission and nuclear fusion.
questions.answer:
NUCLEAR FISSION is the SPLITTING of the nucleus of a heavy atom (such as uranium-235) into smaller nuclei when it is struck by a neutron. It releases a large amount of energy plus more neutrons, which can split further nuclei in a CHAIN REACTION. Fission is the process used in nuclear power plants and is comparatively easy to carry out and control.
NUCLEAR FUSION is the JOINING of two LIGHT nuclei (such as hydrogen) to form a heavier nucleus, releasing even more energy. Fusion is the process that powers the Sun and other stars, but it requires extremely high temperatures and is very difficult to achieve and control on Earth.
questions.explanation: Fission splits heavy nuclei (reactors); fusion joins light nuclei (the Sun).

questions.question: State two hazards of using nuclear energy.
questions.answer: Two hazards of nuclear energy are: (1) Nuclear power plants produce RADIOACTIVE WASTE that remains dangerous for a very long time and must be stored and disposed of very carefully; if it leaks it can contaminate the environment. (2) Accidents or leaks at a plant can release harmful RADIATION, which can cause serious damage to living tissue (radiation sickness, cancers) and to plants, animals and the surroundings.
questions.explanation: Radioactive waste and the danger of radiation leaks/accidents.

questions.question: Why is energy conservation important? Suggest two ways to conserve energy at home.
questions.answer:
Energy conservation is important because most of the energy we use comes from LIMITED, non-renewable fossil fuels whose burning causes pollution and global warming. Using energy efficiently makes these reserves last longer, reduces pollution and saves money.
Two ways to conserve energy at home: (1) Switch off lights, fans and appliances when they are not in use, and use energy-efficient LED/CFL lamps and star-rated appliances. (2) Reduce wasteful use - for example, use natural light during the day, insulate the home, and prefer public transport, cycling or walking over private vehicles where possible.
questions.explanation: Limited fossil reserves + pollution -> conserve; switch off appliances, use efficient devices.

questions.question: What is meant by a renewable source of energy? Give two examples.
questions.answer: A RENEWABLE source of energy is one that is continuously replenished by nature and does not get exhausted with use - it can be used again and again. Examples: solar energy, wind energy (also hydro, tidal, geothermal and biomass energy).

questions.question: Why is no single source of energy considered 'perfect'? Explain with reference to the characteristics of a good source.
questions.answer: A good source of energy should give a large amount of energy per unit mass, be easily and cheaply available, be safe to store and transport, and cause little pollution. In practice every source fails at least one of these: fossil fuels give much energy and are easy to use but are limited and highly polluting; solar and wind are clean and renewable but are dilute, not always available (night, calm days) and need costly equipment; nuclear energy gives huge energy from little fuel but produces dangerous radioactive waste. Because no source meets all the conditions at once, we use a combination of sources suited to each need.

questions.question: State three harmful effects of burning fossil fuels on the environment.
questions.answer: (1) Burning fossil fuels releases CARBON DIOXIDE (CO2), a greenhouse gas that causes GLOBAL WARMING and climate change. (2) It releases oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (SO2 and NO2), which dissolve in rain to cause ACID RAIN that damages plants, soil, buildings and aquatic life. (3) Incomplete combustion produces CARBON MONOXIDE (CO) and SOOT/particulate matter, which pollute the air and harm human health (breathing problems).

questions.question: Name three fractions obtained from petroleum and a use of each.
questions.answer: Three fractions of petroleum and their uses: (1) PETROL - fuel for cars and two-wheelers; (2) DIESEL - fuel for trucks, buses and generators; (3) KEROSENE - fuel for lamps, stoves and jet aircraft. (Other fractions include LPG for cooking, lubricating oil and bitumen for roads.)

questions.question: Trace the energy conversions that take place when coal is used to produce electricity in a thermal power plant.
questions.answer: When coal is burnt in a thermal power plant the following energy conversions occur: (1) the CHEMICAL energy stored in the coal is released as HEAT energy when the coal burns; (2) this heat boils water and produces high-pressure steam, so the heat energy is carried by the steam; (3) the steam strikes the turbine blades and turns them, converting heat energy into MECHANICAL (rotational) energy; (4) the rotating turbine drives a generator, which converts the mechanical energy into ELECTRICAL energy. In short: chemical -> heat -> mechanical -> electrical.

questions.question: Why are thermal power plants usually set up near coalfields?
questions.answer: Thermal power plants burn very large quantities of coal. Transporting such huge amounts of coal over long distances is expensive and difficult. By locating the plant NEAR the coalfield, the cost and effort of transporting the fuel are greatly reduced, making the generation of electricity more economical.

questions.question: Explain how a solar cooker traps heat and why it works only in sunlight.
questions.answer:
A box-type solar cooker has a blackened inner surface, a glass cover and a mirror reflector. Sunlight enters through the glass and is absorbed by the BLACK inner surface, which heats up. The glass cover allows visible sunlight in but does not let the heat (infrared) escape easily - this is the GREENHOUSE EFFECT - so heat accumulates inside and the temperature rises to about 100-140 degrees C, enough to cook food.
It works only in sunlight because its only energy input is the Sun's rays. On a cloudy day or at night there is no sunlight to absorb, so no heat is produced and the cooker cannot work.

questions.question: State two advantages and one limitation of solar cells.
questions.answer: Advantages: (1) Solar cells convert sunlight directly into electricity and cause NO pollution; (2) they have NO moving parts, need little maintenance and last a long time, so they are useful in remote places and satellites. Limitation: they are COSTLY to manufacture, and they produce electricity only when sunlight is available (not at night or on cloudy days).

questions.question: What is a solar panel and why are many cells joined to form one?
questions.answer: A SOLAR PANEL is a number of solar (photovoltaic) cells joined together. A single solar cell produces only a very small voltage and current, which is not enough for most uses. By connecting many cells together in a panel, their outputs add up to give a useful amount of voltage and power that can run appliances, charge batteries or feed electricity into a system.

questions.question: How is electricity generated from wind energy? State one advantage and one limitation.
questions.answer:
Wind (moving air) possesses kinetic energy. In a WIND GENERATOR, the wind strikes large blades mounted on a tall tower and rotates them. This rotating motion is used to turn a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity. Many such windmills set up together form a WIND ENERGY FARM.
Advantage: wind energy is clean, renewable and free, and produces no pollution. Limitation: it works only in windy areas where the wind speed is high enough (about 15 km/h or more), needs large open spaces and high initial cost, and its output varies with the strength of the wind.

questions.question: Describe how tidal energy and ocean thermal energy (OTEC) are obtained from the sea.
questions.answer:
TIDAL ENERGY: The level of sea water rises and falls regularly because of tides. A dam is built across a narrow opening to the sea; as the tide rises and falls, water flows in and out through turbines fitted in the dam, and the moving water turns the turbines to generate electricity.
OCEAN THERMAL ENERGY (OTEC): The surface water of the ocean is warmer than the deep water. An OTEC plant uses this TEMPERATURE DIFFERENCE (about 20 degrees C) - the warm surface water boils a volatile liquid such as ammonia, whose vapour turns a turbine; the cold deep water is then used to condense the vapour back into liquid so the cycle repeats.

questions.question: What is geothermal energy and how is it used to generate electricity?
questions.answer: GEOTHERMAL energy is the heat present inside the Earth. In certain regions called HOT SPOTS, this heat raises the temperature of underground water and turns it into steam. Where the steam comes near the surface, it is tapped through pipes and used to run a turbine connected to a generator, producing electricity. Geothermal energy is renewable and clean, but it can be used only at the few places where hot spots occur.

questions.question: Describe the working of a biogas plant from the dung mixture to the gas and the slurry.
questions.answer: In a biogas plant, cow dung is first mixed with water in a MIXING TANK to form a slurry. The slurry flows into a sealed, dome-shaped underground DIGESTER. There, in the ABSENCE of air, anaerobic bacteria decompose the organic matter over a few weeks. This fermentation produces BIOGAS, a mixture that is about 65-75% methane, which collects in the upper part of the plant and is taken out through a GAS OUTLET pipe for cooking or lighting. The decomposed material (spent slurry) flows out through an OUTLET/OVERFLOW tank and is collected and used as a good manure for crops.

questions.question: State two advantages of using biogas as a fuel.
questions.answer: Two advantages of biogas: (1) it is a CLEAN, SMOKELESS fuel (mainly methane) that gives a high heat output and does not pollute the air like burning wood or dung; (2) it is made from waste such as cow dung and farm waste (a renewable resource), and the leftover slurry is an excellent manure rich in nitrogen and phosphorus, so nothing is wasted.

questions.question: Why is biogas considered a better fuel than directly burning cow dung cakes?
questions.answer: When cow dung cakes are burnt directly, they give a lot of SMOKE, burn incompletely, give relatively little usable heat, and waste the nutrients in the dung. Biogas, made from the same dung by anaerobic decomposition, is mainly methane: it burns CLEANLY and without smoke, gives MORE heat, is convenient to use through pipes, and additionally leaves behind a nutrient-rich slurry that can be used as manure. So biogas makes far better use of the same raw material.

questions.question: What is nuclear fission? Explain how it is used in a nuclear power plant.
questions.answer:
NUCLEAR FISSION is the splitting of the nucleus of a heavy atom (such as uranium-235) into smaller nuclei when it is struck by a neutron. The reaction releases a very large amount of energy and additional neutrons, which split more nuclei in a CHAIN REACTION.
In a NUCLEAR POWER PLANT, this chain reaction is CONTROLLED inside a reactor so that energy is released steadily. The heat produced by fission is used to convert water into steam; the steam drives a turbine connected to a generator, which produces electricity. Thus only the source of heat (fission) differs from a thermal plant - the rest of the process (steam -> turbine -> generator) is the same.

questions.question: State one advantage and one hazard of nuclear energy.
questions.answer: Advantage: a very SMALL amount of nuclear fuel (such as uranium) releases an ENORMOUS amount of energy, and during operation no carbon dioxide or smoke is produced. Hazard: a nuclear plant produces RADIOACTIVE WASTE that stays dangerous for a very long time, and any leak or accident can release harmful radiation that damages living things and the environment.

questions.question: Compare nuclear fission and nuclear fusion in terms of what happens to the nuclei.
questions.answer: In nuclear FISSION, a single HEAVY nucleus (such as uranium-235) is SPLIT into two or more smaller nuclei when hit by a neutron, releasing energy and more neutrons. In nuclear FUSION, two LIGHT nuclei (such as hydrogen) JOIN together to form a single heavier nucleus, releasing even more energy. So fission breaks a big nucleus apart, while fusion combines small nuclei. Fission is used in nuclear reactors on Earth; fusion is the process that powers the Sun and is very difficult to control on Earth.

questions.question: Why is it necessary to conserve energy? Give three reasons.
questions.answer: Energy conservation is necessary because: (1) Most of the energy we use comes from FOSSIL FUELS, which are LIMITED in stock and are being exhausted; conserving them makes the reserves last longer for future generations. (2) Burning fossil fuels causes POLLUTION and GLOBAL WARMING; using less energy reduces these harmful effects on the environment. (3) Energy (electricity and fuel) costs MONEY, so using it efficiently SAVES money for families and the country. For these reasons we should use energy wisely and avoid wasting it.

questions.question: Suggest two simple steps a student can take to save energy at home and school.
questions.answer: Two simple energy-saving steps: (1) SWITCH OFF lights, fans, computers and other appliances when leaving a room or when they are not in use, and use energy-efficient LED/CFL bulbs in place of ordinary bulbs. (2) Make good use of NATURAL LIGHT during the day, walk or cycle for short distances or use public transport, and avoid keeping taps and appliances running unnecessarily.

questions.question: How does shifting to renewable sources of energy help the environment?
questions.answer: Shifting to renewable sources such as solar, wind, hydro and biogas helps the environment because these sources cause LITTLE OR NO POLLUTION - they do not release carbon dioxide, smoke or acid-rain gases the way fossil fuels do. This reduces global warming and air pollution. Renewables are also INEXHAUSTIBLE, so using them saves the limited fossil-fuel reserves for the future and reduces the damage caused by mining and burning fuels.

questions.question: Classify the following as renewable or non-renewable: coal, wind, natural gas, solar energy.
questions.answer: Coal - NON-RENEWABLE (a fossil fuel, limited stock). Wind - RENEWABLE (continuously available). Natural gas - NON-RENEWABLE (a fossil fuel). Solar energy - RENEWABLE (continuously supplied by the Sun).

questions.question: Petrol and diesel are widely used as fuels but are not considered ideal. Give two reasons.
questions.answer: Petrol and diesel (petroleum products) are not ideal fuels because: (1) they are obtained from PETROLEUM, a non-renewable fossil fuel that is LIMITED and will be exhausted; and (2) burning them causes POLLUTION - they release carbon dioxide (global warming), oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (acid rain), and carbon monoxide and soot that harm health. A good fuel should be plentiful and clean, which these are not.

questions.question: Hydroelectric power is renewable and clean, yet building large dams is sometimes opposed. Why?
questions.answer: Although hydroelectric power itself is renewable and pollution-free, building a large dam has serious drawbacks. A large reservoir SUBMERGES vast areas of farmland and FORESTS, destroying habitats and biodiversity. It also DISPLACES many people from their homes and villages, and it can disturb the natural flow of the river and harm aquatic life such as fish. These social and ecological costs are why large dams are sometimes opposed.

questions.question: A region with little sunshine and no rivers is considering a nuclear power plant. Discuss one benefit and two precautions.
questions.answer:
Benefit: a nuclear power plant can supply a LARGE and steady amount of electricity from a very SMALL quantity of fuel, and unlike solar or hydro it does not depend on sunshine or flowing water, so it suits a region lacking those. During operation it also releases no carbon dioxide or smoke.
Precautions: (1) the RADIOACTIVE WASTE produced must be stored and disposed of very safely so it does not leak and contaminate the surroundings; (2) the reactor must have strong safety systems and trained staff to prevent ACCIDENTS and radiation leaks, which could cause serious harm to people and the environment. Proper site selection and shielding are essential.

questions.question: Both a thermal plant and a hydroelectric plant turn a turbine. How do the two differ in the way the turbine is driven and in their effect on the environment?
questions.answer:
In a THERMAL plant, the turbine is driven by HIGH-PRESSURE STEAM produced by burning a fossil fuel (coal). Burning the fuel releases carbon dioxide, sulphur and nitrogen oxides and soot, so a thermal plant POLLUTES the air and contributes to global warming and acid rain.
In a HYDROELECTRIC plant, the turbine is driven by FALLING WATER stored behind a dam - no fuel is burnt, so there is no air pollution or CO2. However, building the dam SUBMERGES land and forests, displaces people and affects river ecosystems. So thermal plants pollute the air, while hydro plants are clean to run but disturb land and water ecosystems.

questions.question: Differentiate between conventional and non-conventional sources of energy with one example each.
questions.answer: CONVENTIONAL sources are those that have been in use for a long time, exist in a LIMITED stock and are non-renewable - for example, coal. NON-CONVENTIONAL sources are newer, renewable sources that are continuously replenished by nature and do not run out - for example, solar energy. Conventional sources (fossil and nuclear fuels) are generally polluting and finite, while non-conventional sources (solar, wind, hydro, biomass, etc.) are cleaner and inexhaustible.

questions.question: What is a solar water heater and how does it work?
questions.answer: A SOLAR WATER HEATER is a device that uses sunlight to heat water for domestic use. It has an insulated storage tank connected to a flat collector made of BLACKENED pipes or plates. Sunlight falls on the black collector, which absorbs the heat and warms the water flowing through the pipes. The hot water rises and collects in the insulated tank, where it stays warm until needed. It is clean, uses free solar energy and saves fuel and electricity, but works best in bright sunshine.

questions.question: What is biomass? Give two examples.
questions.answer: BIOMASS is organic matter obtained from plants and animals that can be used as a source of energy. It includes living or recently living material and the wastes from it. Examples: wood (and crop residues such as straw), and cow dung (animal waste). Biomass can be burnt directly for heat or, better, converted into a clean fuel such as biogas.

questions.question: All methods of producing energy affect the environment in some way. Justify this statement with three examples.
questions.answer: Every way of producing energy has some environmental cost. (1) Burning FOSSIL FUELS in thermal plants and vehicles releases carbon dioxide (global warming), oxides of sulphur and nitrogen (acid rain) and soot - causing air pollution. (2) Building large DAMS for hydroelectric power submerges land and forests, displaces people and disturbs aquatic life. (3) NUCLEAR power plants produce radioactive waste that stays dangerous for a long time and can cause radiation hazards if it leaks. Even 'clean' renewables need land and materials. So no method is completely free of impact, which is why we must use energy carefully and prefer the least harmful sources.

questions.question: A town gets all its electricity from a coal-based thermal power plant. Residents notice the air is often smoky, nearby ponds have become acidic, and the coal stock is shrinking each year. (a) Why is the coal stock shrinking and not refilling? (b) What causes the smoky air? (c) What makes the ponds acidic? (d) Suggest one cleaner alternative for generating the town's electricity.
questions.answer: (a) Coal is a FOSSIL FUEL formed over millions of years from buried plant remains. It is NON-RENEWABLE, so once burnt it cannot be replaced within a human timescale - the stock keeps shrinking as it is used. (b) Burning coal, especially when combustion is incomplete, releases SOOT (carbon particles) and smoke that make the air smoky and harm health. (c) Coal contains sulphur and nitrogen; on burning, these form oxides (SO2 and NO2) that dissolve in rain to form ACID RAIN, which makes the ponds acidic. (d) A cleaner alternative is a renewable source such as a SOLAR power plant (solar panels) or a WIND energy farm, which generate electricity without burning fuel and so cause little pollution.
questions.explanation: Tests understanding of fossil-fuel depletion, smoke/soot, acid rain and renewable alternatives.

questions.question: Riya installs a box-type solar cooker (black box, glass cover, mirror) and a set of solar panels on her roof. The cooker heats up well at noon but does nothing after sunset, and the panels stop producing power at night. (a) Why does the cooker get hot at noon? (b) What is the role of the glass cover? (c) Why do both devices stop working after sunset? (d) Name the device that converts sunlight directly into electricity.
questions.answer: (a) At noon the Sun is overhead and bright; the black inner surface of the cooker absorbs the strong sunlight and gets hot, and the mirror reflects extra sunlight in. (b) The GLASS COVER lets sunlight in but does not allow the heat (infrared) to escape easily - the GREENHOUSE EFFECT - so heat is trapped and the temperature rises. (c) Both devices depend entirely on SUNLIGHT as their energy input. After sunset there is no sunlight, so the cooker gets no heat and the panels get no light to convert - hence both stop working. This shows a key limitation of solar energy: it is available only in the daytime. (d) The SOLAR CELL (photovoltaic cell), many of which make up a solar panel, converts sunlight directly into electricity.
questions.explanation: Applies the greenhouse effect, the role of glass, the daytime limitation of solar energy, and the photovoltaic cell.

questions.question: A farmer sets up a biogas plant. He mixes cow dung with water and feeds it into a sealed underground tank. After about two weeks a smokeless gas comes out through a pipe and he uses it for cooking; a thick slurry flows out from the other end. (a) Name the sealed tank where the gas is formed. (b) In what condition (with or without air) is the gas formed? (c) Name the main gas present in biogas. (d) What useful purpose does the slurry serve?
questions.answer: (a) The sealed underground tank where the gas is formed is the DIGESTER. (b) The gas is formed in the ABSENCE of air - it is produced by ANAEROBIC bacteria that decompose the dung slurry. (c) The main gas present in biogas is METHANE (CH4), which makes up about 65-75% of it and burns without smoke. (d) The leftover SLURRY is used as MANURE (fertiliser); it is rich in nitrogen and phosphorus and improves the fertility of the soil, so nothing is wasted and the farm waste is safely used up.
questions.explanation: Applies the parts and working of a biogas plant: digester, anaerobic decomposition, methane and slurry as manure.

questions.question: A country plans a new nuclear power plant. Engineers say a few kilograms of uranium can supply electricity for a whole city for a long time and that the plant will release no smoke or carbon dioxide. Local people worry about safety and waste. (a) Which nuclear process is used in the plant? (b) Why can so little fuel supply so much energy? (c) Why does the plant release no CO2 or smoke? (d) State one safety concern the people are right to raise.
questions.answer: (a) The plant uses NUCLEAR FISSION - the controlled splitting of heavy uranium-235 nuclei in a reactor, which proceeds as a chain reaction. (b) When a nucleus undergoes fission, it releases an ENORMOUS amount of energy compared with ordinary chemical reactions like burning. So even a few kilograms of uranium can release as much energy as huge quantities of coal, supplying a city for a long time. (c) The plant does NOT burn any fuel; the heat comes from fission of the nucleus, not from combustion. Since no fuel is burnt, no carbon dioxide or smoke is produced during operation. (d) The people are right to worry about RADIOACTIVE WASTE and the risk of radiation leaks/accidents: the waste stays dangerous for a very long time and must be stored very safely, and any leak could release harmful radiation that damages living things and the environment.
questions.explanation: Evaluates the benefits and hazards of nuclear fission energy: high energy density, no CO2, but radioactive waste and radiation risk.

questions.question: A coastal village has strong winds, high tides, a hilly river nearby and abundant sunshine, but no fossil fuels. A committee wants to use only renewable sources. (a) Name the device that can use the strong winds to make electricity. (b) How can the river be used to generate electricity? (c) Name the energy source that uses the rise and fall of the tides. (d) State one advantage common to all these sources.
questions.answer: (a) A WINDMILL (wind generator) - many of them together form a wind energy farm - can use the strong winds to generate electricity. (b) The hilly river can be dammed to store water at a HEIGHT; when the water falls it turns a turbine connected to a generator, producing HYDROELECTRIC power. (c) The rise and fall of the tides can be used as TIDAL ENERGY: water flowing in and out through turbines in a tidal dam generates electricity. (d) One advantage common to wind, hydro and tidal energy is that they are RENEWABLE and cause little or no pollution - they do not get exhausted and do not release carbon dioxide or smoke like fossil fuels.
questions.explanation: Analyses the suitable renewable options for a coastal/hilly site: wind, hydro and tidal energy, and their common renewable, clean nature.

questions.question: A teacher writes on the board: coal, solar energy, petroleum, wind, natural gas, biogas. She asks the class to sort them and to comment on their qualities as energy sources. (a) Which of these are non-renewable? (b) Which are renewable? (c) Why are the non-renewable ones a cause of concern? (d) State one quality that makes a source 'good'.
questions.answer: (a) NON-RENEWABLE: coal, petroleum and natural gas - these are fossil fuels with a limited stock. (b) RENEWABLE: solar energy, wind and biogas - these are continuously replenished by nature. (c) The non-renewable sources are a concern because they exist in LIMITED amounts and take millions of years to form, so they will be EXHAUSTED; also, burning them POLLUTES the air and causes global warming and acid rain. (d) A good source of energy should release a large amount of energy per unit mass, be easily and cheaply available, be safe to store and transport, and cause little or no pollution (any one of these qualities is acceptable).
questions.explanation: Classifies sources, explains the concern over finite polluting fuels, and recalls a quality of a good source.

questions.question: In a thermal power station, coal is burnt in a boiler, water is turned into steam, the steam spins a large wheel, and a connected machine produces electricity. (a) What is the 'large wheel' called? (b) What is the connected machine that produces electricity called? (c) Write the full sequence of energy conversions. (d) Name one pollutant released by this plant.
questions.answer: (a) The large wheel spun by the steam is the TURBINE. (b) The connected machine that produces electricity is the GENERATOR. (c) The sequence of energy conversions is: CHEMICAL energy (in coal) -> HEAT energy (in steam) -> MECHANICAL energy (rotation of the turbine) -> ELECTRICAL energy (output of the generator). (d) Pollutants released include carbon dioxide (CO2), oxides of sulphur (SO2) and nitrogen (NO2), and soot/smoke (any one is acceptable).
questions.explanation: Identifies turbine and generator, the chemical-heat-mechanical-electrical chain, and a pollutant.

questions.question: An island far out at sea has no fossil fuels and no rivers, but has very warm surface water, cold deep water, strong sea waves and underground hot springs. (a) Which energy system uses the temperature difference between warm surface and cold deep water? (b) Which source uses the motion of sea waves? (c) Which source uses the underground hot springs? (d) Give one common advantage of all these sources.
questions.answer: (a) The temperature difference between the warm surface water and the cold deep water is used by an OTEC plant (Ocean Thermal Energy Conversion). (b) The motion of sea waves is used as WAVE ENERGY, in which the moving waves drive turbines. (c) The underground hot springs are a form of GEOTHERMAL energy: the steam from the hot spots can run a turbine to make electricity. (d) A common advantage is that all of them are RENEWABLE and clean - they do not run out and cause little or no pollution, unlike fossil fuels.
questions.explanation: Evaluates which marine/geothermal source fits each clue and their shared renewable, clean nature.

questions.question: A science magazine says: 'The Sun shines because tiny nuclei join together deep inside it, while on Earth power stations split big nuclei to make electricity.' (a) Name the process happening in the Sun. (b) Name the process used in Earth's nuclear power stations. (c) Which of the two is harder to control on Earth? (d) State one benefit of nuclear power stations.
questions.answer: (a) The process happening in the Sun is NUCLEAR FUSION - light nuclei (hydrogen) join to form a heavier nucleus, releasing energy. (b) The process used in Earth's nuclear power stations is NUCLEAR FISSION - heavy nuclei such as uranium-235 are split. (c) FUSION is harder to control on Earth because it needs extremely high temperatures and conditions that are very difficult to achieve and maintain. (d) A benefit of nuclear power stations is that a very small amount of fuel releases an enormous amount of energy, and during operation they release no carbon dioxide or smoke.
questions.explanation: Distinguishes fusion (Sun) and fission (reactors), notes fusion is hard to control, and a benefit of nuclear power.

questions.question: A family's electricity bill keeps rising. They use old bulbs, leave fans and the TV on when out, and drive a car even for short trips to the market. (a) Why is energy conservation good for this family? (b) Suggest a change to their lighting. (c) Suggest a change to their short trips. (d) How does conserving energy help the whole country and environment?
questions.answer: (a) Conserving energy is good for the family because it will lower their electricity and fuel bills (SAVING money) and reduce wasteful use. (b) They should replace the old bulbs with energy-efficient LED or CFL lamps, which give the same light using much less electricity, and switch off lights, fans and the TV when not in use. (c) For short trips to the market they could WALK, CYCLE or use public transport instead of the car, which saves fuel. (d) For the country and environment, conserving energy makes the LIMITED fossil-fuel reserves last longer and reduces the pollution and global warming caused by burning fuel, so the air is cleaner and resources are saved for the future.
questions.explanation: Evaluates personal energy-saving steps and links conservation to national and environmental benefits.
